title: Heroic Hindu Resistance to Muslim Invaders, 636–1206
byline: by Sita Ram Goel · Voice of India · a long review of R.G. Misra's Indian Resistance to Early Muslim Invaders up to 1206 A.D. (1983)
lede: Goel challenges the idea that India was a passive land invaders walked into, summed up in Matthew Arnold's line that the East “let the legions thunder past.” He follows the historian R.G. Misra, chapter by chapter. Armies that took Syria in six months and Persia in a few years needed 570 years to set up a lasting state in northern India. Then Goel draws lessons for the 1980s.
facts: from the first Arab expedition against Thana (636) to the Delhi Sultanate (1206)
the Arabs spent failing in Sindh before Muhammad bin Qasim took it in 712
of effective Muslim rule over northern India, to Aurangzeb's death in 1707, per Misra
Hindus said by a Muslim chronicler to have died defending Somnath in 1026
note: The book is a review with a political argument attached. The battle narrative follows Misra, who relies on Muslim chroniclers such as Firishta and on Sanskrit inscriptions. Casualty figures are the chroniclers'. The closing chapters on Pakistan are Goel's own view and are attributed to him.

sections.title: How long the conquests took
sections.lede: Years from the first serious campaign to lasting control, using the dates the book gives. India is the outlier the book sets out to explain.
items: Defeated in 637, overrun “in the next few years”; Caliphate reaches India's borders by 643
From Egypt (640) to crossing into Spain (709)
Thana raid (636) to the Delhi Sultanate (1206)
sections.note: Spans are worked out from dates in the book (following Misra), as a rough comparison, not exact figures.

sections.title: From Thana to Tarain
items: Naval raids on Thana and Broach repulsed
Under Caliph Umar. Mughairah's attack on Debal also fails.
“The four pious Caliphs” die without a victory over Sindh.
All repulsed but the last, which takes Makran.
Arab generals defeated or killed, and ransom paid for one.
Muhammad bin Qasim takes Sindh and Multan
Recalled in 714. India “threw off their yoke”.
Defeated by Pulakesin of the Chalukyas at Navsari and held off by Lalitaditya of Kashmir.
Their eclipse is not caused by the Arabs.
Released, he burns himself on a pyre rather than rule after defeat.
Mahmud breaks the image, after a battle “long doubtful”.
Raja of Delhi retakes Hansi, Thanesar, Kangra
Inflicts “one of the worst defeats” on the Muslims.
Ghuri wins after an offer of truce, which Goel calls “perfidy where valour failed”.
He had stayed out of the earlier wars.
The Mher Rajputs rise, Kanauj is retaken (1197), and Bhimadeva II recovers Gujarat (1201).
Bakhtiyar Khalji in Bihar and Bengal
He cannot take East Bengal, and Assam stays free.

sections.eyebrow: Chapter 5 · why the Hindus lost, per Misra
sections.title: Not disunity, but the lack of a strategy
sections.lede: Misra rejects the usual explanation. Internal feuds, he says, were “a common feature of the Middle Ages everywhere”.

items: No forward policy: wars fought at home, never carried into the enemy's base
No central government for northern India
Alliances that came apart after each battle
Slow elephant armies and no standing army
A steady inflow of Arabs and Turks

sections.title: From Tarain to Pakistan
items: Its rulers celebrate Mahmud and Ghuri, so Goel argues India should read its hostility as ideology, not just border politics.
India now has the standing army and central government the Rajputs lacked, Goel says, but not the self-awareness.
He calls for a politics “created by Hindu consciousness” instead of vote-bank parties.
Push India's own ideological frontiers outward, with humanist and rationalist allies even in Muslim countries.
